issues.legal_issue: An agreement imposing revised mining royalty terms is not void under the 1913 mining rules where those rules were not statutory, or where the Governor acted as grantor and could authorize an exception to them.
material_facts: The parties entered into an agreement requiring payment of royalty at an enhanced rate in return for permission to consolidate and work additional mining areas.
The agreement showed that the Governor was in the position of lessor and grantor.
The appellants ultimately conceded that the 1913 rules were not statutory.
issues.conclusion: The agreement was not void under the 1913 rules, and its revised terms were binding.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the 1913 rules were not statutory. It also reasoned that, even assuming the rules had statutory force and applied, Rule 1 permitted exceptions with the requisite governmental sanction; after the constitutional changes, the Governor could exercise the relevant authority. Because the Governor was in the position of grantor, it was to be presumed that he decided the revised terms were in the State’s interest. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.royalty_contract_validity_challenge: The proceeding challenges whether an agreement imposing mining royalty terms is valid and binding.
predicates.mining_rules_not_statutory: The rules governing the grant of mining leases were not statutory rules.
predicates.governor_was_grantor: The Governor acted in the position of grantor of the mining lease.
predicates.revised_royalty_terms_are_binding: The revised royalty terms in the agreement bind the parties.

issues.definition: When a mining royalty agreement is challenged and the governing rules are nonstatutory or the Governor acted as grantor, the revised royalty terms bind the parties.

issues.legal_issue: Rules that became effective after a mining agreement was finalized do not invalidate the agreement by retrospective application.
material_facts: The agreement was finalized before the 1949 mineral concession rules came into effect.
The appellants worked the mines with the Government’s permission during a period ending before those rules came into effect.
The 1949 rules had no retrospective effect.
issues.conclusion: The 1949 rules did not apply to the agreement or the mining operations at issue, so they did not invalidate the agreed royalty terms.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1948 required mining leases granted after the relevant commencement to conform to rules made under the Act. The Mineral Concession Rules, 1949 came into effect on October 25, 1949 and had no retrospective effect; the Court held that no such rules were in existence during the period relevant to the dispute. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.challenge_to_pre_effective_mining_agreem: The proceeding challenges a mining agreement finalized before the relevant mining rules took effect.
predicates.agreement_finalized_before_rules_effecti: The parties finalized the mining agreement before the rules at issue became effective.
predicates.rules_not_retroactive: The rules at issue do not apply retrospectively.
predicates.later_rules_do_not_invalidate_agreement: Rules that took effect later do not invalidate the earlier agreement.

issues.definition: When a proceeding challenges a mining agreement finalized before applicable rules took effect, and those rules are not retrospective, the later rules do not invalidate the agreement.

issues.legal_issue: A mining royalty agreement is not vitiated merely because a proposed general policy or rule change was not ultimately adopted, where the parties knowingly negotiated and accepted the agreement without coercion, undue influence, or mutual mistake.
material_facts: The Government had published a draft amendment to mining rules inviting objections, but the draft was not finalized.
The appellants negotiated with the Government and accepted the enhanced royalty terms while seeking to acquire additional mining areas and begin mining operations.
The appellants entered the agreement with knowledge of its terms; the agreement was not challenged on the basis of coercion, undue influence, or mutual mistake.
issues.conclusion: The alleged representation about a future general increase in royalty rates did not provide a basis for setting aside the agreement.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the non-finalization of a draft amendment did not give the appellants a cause of action to avoid the agreement. The parties had discussed and knowingly accepted its terms, and no coercion, undue influence, or mutual mistake was established. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this issue.

rule.if: misrepresentation_based_contract_challenge and proposed_policy_not_finalized and terms_knowingly_negotiated and no_coercion_or_mutual_mistake

predicates.misrepresentation_based_contract_challen: The proceeding seeks to avoid a contract on the basis of an alleged representation about future governmental policy.
predicates.proposed_policy_not_finalized: A proposed policy or rule change was not ultimately finalized.
predicates.terms_knowingly_negotiated: The parties discussed the contract terms and one party accepted them with knowledge of their content.
predicates.no_coercion_or_mutual_mistake: The contract was not shown to have resulted from coercion or mutual mistake, and no undue influence was established.
predicates.agreement_not_vitiated_by_alleged_misrep: The alleged representation does not vitiate the agreement.

issues.definition: When a contract is challenged based on an alleged future-policy representation, but the proposal was not finalized and the terms were knowingly negotiated without coercion or mutual mistake, the agreement is not vitiated by that allegation.

issues.legal_issue: A State’s collection of payment due under an enforceable contract does not deprive the payer of property without authority of law.
material_facts: The appellants paid the disputed royalty under protest.
The payment was recoverable by the Government under the agreement.
The Court found that the agreement was enforceable and not vitiated.
issues.conclusion: The State had not deprived the appellants of property within the meaning of Article 31(1) of the Constitution.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31(1) of the Constitution prohibited deprivation of property without authority of law. The Court held that payment recoverable under an enforceable, unvitiated contract was not a deprivation of property by the State within that prohibition. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.constitutional_property_deprivation_clai: The proceeding claims that the State deprived a person of property without lawful authority.
predicates.payment_due_under_enforceable_contract: The disputed payment was due under a contract that remained enforceable.
predicates.contractual_collection_is_not_unlawful_p: Collection of the contractual payment is not an unlawful deprivation of property.

issues.definition: When a property-deprivation claim concerns payment due under an enforceable contract, collection of that payment is not an unlawful deprivation of property.
